Parallelism means the state or quality of two or more things being parallel — existing, running, or developing alongside each other in a similar, matching, or corresponding way.

Think of train tracks. They run side by side, always the same distance apart, never meeting. That image — things mirroring each other, moving in the same direction, staying matched — is the root idea behind every use of this word.

Now let's look at how it actually appears across different areas of life, because this word shows up in several important contexts.
1. Parallelism in Writing and Grammar (the most common use)

When you list things or connect ideas in a sentence, they should be "matched" in grammatical form — like items in a set that belong together.

Broken parallelism (wrong):
"She loves to read, writing, and to swim."
The three items don't match: "to read," "writing," "to swim" — three different forms fighting each other.

With parallelism (right):
"She loves to read, to write, and to swim."
or
"She loves reading, writing, and swimming."
Now all three items are in the same form.

Why does this matter? Parallelism makes writing feel balanced, rhythmic, and easy to follow. When the structure is inconsistent, the reader feels a small jolt — like a hiccup in the rhythm. When it's consistent, reading flows naturally.

Famous examples:

Caesar's "I came, I saw, I conquered."
Each clause has the same form: subject + verb. That matching structure is parallelism — and it's part of why the phrase feels so punchy and memorable.

JFK's "Ask not what your country can do for you — ask what you can do for your country."
The two halves mirror each other almost perfectly. That deliberate mirroring is parallelism at work.

Parallelism also applies beyond sentences. Across paragraphs or a whole essay, writers use parallel structures to signal that ideas are equal in importance or belong in the same category.

In a broader literary sense, parallelism refers to any deliberate repetition of structure or form — used to create rhythm, emphasis, or balance.

Poets use it constantly. When lines in a poem follow a similar rhythm or structure, that's parallelism. It gives writing a sense of order and power.

It also applies to storytelling. If a novel has two separate storylines that unfold alongside each other — each one reflecting or echoing the other — that structural mirroring is also called parallelism (often specifically called a "parallel plot").

In computing, parallelism means doing multiple tasks at the same time, instead of one after another.

Normally, a computer handles things sequentially — task 1, then task 2, then task 3. With parallelism, it splits the work across multiple processors and tackles several tasks simultaneously. This makes computation dramatically faster.

For example: if you need to process one million images, doing them one by one would take a long time. With parallelism, you might split the work across 100 processors and finish roughly 100 times faster.

This is why modern computers and phones have "multi-core" processors — they're built to take advantage of parallelism.

In philosophy — particularly in discussions about the mind and body — psychophysical parallelism is the view that mental events (your thoughts and feelings) and physical events (activity in your brain) happen alongside each other in perfect correspondence, but neither one causes the other. They simply run in parallel, like two clocks ticking in sync without one driving the other.

This is one answer to the famous "mind-body problem": how do your thoughts relate to your brain? Parallelism says they correspond, but neither is the boss of the other.

In evolutionary biology, parallel evolution (also called parallelism) refers to when two separate species, evolving independently in similar environments, develop similar traits — without one descending from the other.

For example, dolphins and sharks have very similar body shapes. Not because one evolved from the other, but because they both live in water and faced similar pressures over time. That independent, side-by-side development of a similar solution is parallelism.

No matter the field, the word always carries the same underlying idea: things that mirror each other, run alongside each other, or correspond to each other in a structured, matching way.

  • In grammar: matching structure within sentences and lists.
  • In literature: repeating form across lines or storylines for rhythm and emphasis.
  • In computing: doing multiple things simultaneously instead of one at a time.
  • In philosophy: mind and body running in correspondence without causing each other.
  • In biology: separate species independently developing similar traits.

Once you hold that central image in your mind — two things running side by side, in step with each other, perfectly matched — every use of the word clicks into place.
